narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 55.6% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three pieces of information about you, ranked by importance. Your LSAT score was the strongest factor and pushed the prediction toward failure. At 27, it sits well below the average of 37 among students who were accepted, signaling weaker preparation for the exam. Your undergraduate GPA was the second most important factor and worked in your favor. At 3.8 it is noticeably higher than the 3.23 average of accepted students, which helped pull the prediction back toward passing. Your third-year class ranking came in third. Placing in the fourth decile (compared to an average around the sixth decile for accepted students) added a modest push toward predicting failure.

Taken together, the lower LSAT score and weaker class rank outweighed your strong college grades, tipping the model just past the threshold for rejection.

What you should do next is clear: retake the LSAT and aim for a substantially higher score. Many students improve dramatically on a second attempt. Once you raise that score, the same model would likely view your application much more favorably. Focus your energy there and reapply.
